Extensive experiments show that the proposed training strategy, which does not require matched reference data, outperforms a state-of-the-art compressed sensing (CS)-based method and delivers results comparable to or better than those of supervised learning approaches.

Among non-contrast MR techniques for depicting blood vessels, time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) is one of the most commonly used. Because it relies on 3-D volume acquisition, however, strong acceleration is required, making accurate reconstruction from undersampled TOF-MRA an important deep-learning problem. A major limitation of many existing deep-learning approaches is their dependence on matched reference data for supervised training, which is often hard to obtain.  

To address this issue, we build on recent cycleGAN theory derived from optimal transport and introduce a new two-stage unsupervised deep-learning framework. The method first applies a multi-coil reconstruction network in the coronal plane, and then uses a multi-planar refinement network in the axial plane. More specifically, the initial network is trained in the square-root of sum of squares (SSoS) domain to produce high-quality parallel image reconstruction. The subsequent refinement network is then designed to efficiently capture the features of highly activated blood flow through a double-headed max-pool discriminator.  

Extensive experiments show that this learning strategy, despite not using matched reference data, outperforms a state-of-the-art compressed sensing (CS)-based method and achieves results comparable to, or even better than, supervised learning approaches.

response_text: This paper advances an interpretation of dropout regularization that is not entirely novel, yet remains insufficiently appreciated in the literature. Rather than treating dropout merely as a heuristic for preventing co-adaptation or as a practical trick for improving generalization, the discussion emphasizes its role as a specific form of stochastic model averaging and implicit regularization. In this view, dropout induces a training procedure over a large ensemble of thinned networks that share parameters, thereby shaping the learned representation in a structured and nontrivial way. The contribution of the paper lies less in proposing a radically new mechanism than in clarifying and sharpening a perspective that has often been invoked only informally. By making this interpretation more explicit, the paper helps explain why dropout can be effective across a range of architectures and settings, while also pointing to limitations in how the method is commonly understood.

Estimating and reducing the overhead of fault tolerance (FT) schemes is a central challenge on the path to scalable quantum computing. While FT is essential for protecting fragile quantum information against noise and operational errors, its practical cost can be enormous, often requiring many additional physical qubits and operations to encode and preserve a much smaller number of logical qubits. Understanding this overhead is therefore not just a theoretical exercise, but a key requirement for determining whether large-scale quantum algorithms can be implemented within realistic hardware constraints.

A careful assessment of FT overhead involves analyzing several interconnected factors, including the choice of error-correcting code, the physical error rates of the underlying device, the architecture of qubit connectivity, and the resources needed for logical gates, measurements, and state preparation. In many cases, the dominant cost arises not only from storing logical information reliably, but also from executing nontrivial operations in a fault-tolerant manner. As a result, overhead estimates must account for both space and time, as well as the tradeoffs between them.

Reducing this overhead requires progress at multiple levels of the stack. Improvements in hardware fidelity can lower the burden placed on error correction, while more efficient codes, decoding strategies, and circuit constructions can decrease the number of required resources. Equally important is the development of realistic benchmarking and modeling tools that connect abstract FT protocols to concrete device capabilities. By combining accurate estimation with targeted optimization, researchers can better identify the most promising routes toward practical, large-scale quantum computation.

response_text:
Cell-free massive MIMO (CF-M-MIMO) systems represent a significant step beyond the classical cellular architecture that has shaped mobile communications for decades. Instead of dividing the coverage area into fixed cells served by individual base stations, CF-M-MIMO relies on a large number of distributed access points that jointly serve users over the same time-frequency resources. This more cooperative structure reduces the notion of cell boundaries and aims to provide a more uniform quality of service across the network.

The main motivation behind this evolution is the growing demand for higher data rates, better reliability, and more consistent user experience. In conventional cellular systems, users located near the edge of a cell often suffer from weaker signal quality and stronger interference. Cell-free massive MIMO addresses this issue by allowing many geographically distributed antennas to coordinate their transmissions and receptions, effectively turning the entire network into a large distributed antenna array. As a result, users can benefit from macro-diversity, improved spectral efficiency, and reduced sensitivity to local shadowing and fading.

At the same time, the advantages of CF-M-MIMO come with important practical challenges. Coordinating many distributed access points requires efficient signal processing, scalable resource allocation, and robust fronthaul connections. Channel estimation, synchronization, and power control also become more complex in such a distributed setting. For this reason, cell-free massive MIMO is not only a new network architecture, but also a research direction that brings together communication theory, optimization, and system design in the effort to support future wireless networks.

In contrast, the present paper establishes through perturbative methods that every analytic metric on $\mathbb{S}^{3}$ that is sufficiently close to the round metric $g_{0}$ admits \textsl{generalized} totally umbilic 2-spheres, that is, critical points of the conformal Willmore functional $\int_{\Sigma}|A^\circ|^{2}\,d\mu_{\gamma}$. An analogous statement also holds for smooth metrics, assuming an appropriate non-degeneracy condition on the traceless Ricci tensor.

It also relies on a quantitative Schur-type Lemma to handle the situation in which the traceless Ricci tensor of the perturbation is degenerate without vanishing identically. As a consequence, for left-invariant metrics on $SU(2)\cong \mathbb{S}^{3}$, the theorem yields the existence of uncountably many distinct Willmore spheres.

contexts. We introduce and analyse such a parameter-free variant for two

In many situations with finite element discretizations it is desirable or necessary to impose boundary or interface conditions not as essential conditions, that is, not by restricting the trial space a priori, but rather in a weak sense through additional variational terms. This viewpoint is especially useful when the boundary data are complicated, when interfaces separate nonmatching meshes or different materials, or when one seeks a formulation that treats several types of conditions in a unified way. Instead of enforcing the constraint pointwise, one augments the weak formulation so that the desired condition is recovered consistently while preserving flexibility in the discrete space.

Such weak imposition can be achieved in several closely related ways. A classical approach introduces Lagrange multipliers, which enforce the condition exactly at the variational level but enlarge the system and require compatibility between spaces. Penalty methods avoid extra unknowns by adding a term that penalizes violations of the constraint, though the choice of penalty parameter affects both accuracy and conditioning. Nitsche-type methods combine consistency and stabilization in a particularly attractive manner, allowing one to impose Dirichlet or interface conditions without modifying the finite element space itself. In practice, these techniques are valuable whenever strong enforcement is inconvenient, unstable, or simply impossible within the chosen discretization.

Even after the Berlin Wall went up in 1961, East Germany was never sealed off in the way North Korea is today. The border regime was harsh and tightly controlled, but there were still many channels of contact across the divide. West German television and radio reached much of the East, millions of family ties continued to exist on both sides, and despite heavy restrictions, letters, parcels, and occasional visits remained part of everyday life for many people.

There was also a broader flow of goods, information, and diplomatic contact than in a truly isolated state. East Germany traded extensively within the Eastern bloc, maintained formal relations with other socialist countries, and over time even developed practical arrangements with West Germany. Travel was limited and politically filtered, especially for ordinary citizens, but the country was not cut off from the outside world in absolute terms.

That does not make the dictatorship mild. Surveillance, censorship, and repression were real, and leaving the country without permission could have severe consequences. But if the comparison is with present-day North Korea, the difference matters: East Germany was authoritarian and closed, yet still embedded in a Europe where exchange across borders never fully disappeared.

In this state, he dreams that he and Alix had once been Scottish slaves aboard Leif Ericson’s ship during its voyage of discovery to Greenland. Part of the dream involves the two slaves leaving behind a stone engraved with their names at the Vikings’ landing site in North America.

Ross recovers and tells Alix and Lockwood about his dream. The last part of the photographic survey is completed successfully, and the three then finish their flight across to North America, arriving in eastern Canada. As they fly south along the coast toward New York, Ross recognizes the place where he had dreamed Leif Ericson’s expedition came ashore on the coast of Cape Cod. They land to investigate and discover the stone bearing the slaves’ names.

"Merle Lindsay Salathiel (1916 – October 12, 1965), better known as Merl Lindsay, was one of the premier American Western swing musicians from the 1930s to the mid-1960s and founder of Merl Lindsay and His Oklahoma Night Riders.
Life and career
Merle Lindsay Salathiel was born in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma to Clarence Earl and Louella Salathiel, early pioneers of the Oklahoma Territory. He began his music career in 1936 playing fiddle in his father (C.E. Salathiel)'s ballroom, Salathiel's Barn. In 1937 he formed his first band, the Barnyard Boys. In 1947, he created a larger band and added a female singer, calling the group Merl Lindsay and His Oklahoma Night Riders. During the 1940s, he owned a ballroom in Compton, California, and broadcast over a four-station radio hookup in Hollywood and Long Beach. He also performed with Jimmy Wakely in Western B-movies.
In 1957, Lindsay joined ABC-TV's Ozark Jubilee, taking over the ten-piece Ozark Jubilee Band. His group adopted the name when the TV program's title was changed to Country Music Jubilee the next year. During later years he toured the US and performed at his ballroom, Lindsayland, in Oklahoma City.
Many famous Western swing musicians performed with Lindsay's bands over the years. Two of his female singers were Wanda Jackson and Norma Jean. His brother, Doyle Salathiel (1920–1976), played with Lindsay's bands as well as others, and was a composer who wrote the words for the band's signature song, "Water Baby Blues". Lindsay's nephew, Max Salathiel (1935–2006), an accomplished Oklahoma City guitar player, also worked with his band in the 1950s, as did his sister Alojah Salathiel.
Other band members included Robert "Buddy" Ray, Rudy Martin, Frederick "Freddie" Loveland, Louvenie Loveland, Ted Haff, Mike Hugo, Clarence Bailey, Homer Bean, Gerald "Buster" Magness, Gene Jones (steel guitar) and Sonny Rogers.
Lindsay was married to Doris Salathiel. He had three children, Merlynn Salathiel, Denzel Salathiel (1952-2016) and Jackie Merle Phillips (1934-2000). Lindsay died in Oklahoma City from cancer on October 12, 1965. He is buried in Sunnylane Cemetery in Del City, Oklahoma.
Compositions 
Lindsay wrote many songs that became hits for himself and other Western swing artists. Among them:
 "Lonesome Okie Goin' Home"
 "Shimmy Shakin' Daddy"
 "Slidin' Steel" (with Gene Crownover)
 "Water Baby Blues/Water Baby Boogie"

The flaw in this logic is that it ignores what actually happens to the money earned by people in the top tax brackets. That income does not simply vanish when taxes are raised, nor does it all remain in some idle personal reserve when taxes are lowered. In practice, high earners spend, invest, shelter, move, and restructure their income in response to incentives. That means the effect of taxation is not just a matter of taking a larger or smaller slice of a fixed pie.

A large share of top-bracket income is tied to capital gains, business profits, stock compensation, and other forms of earnings that are highly sensitive to tax treatment. When rates rise, some income is deferred, reclassified, or shifted into tax-advantaged channels. When rates fall, some of that income becomes more visible and more taxable. So the headline rate alone does not tell you how much revenue will actually be collected, or how much economic activity will be affected.

There is also the question of where the money goes after taxes are paid. Tax revenue is not destroyed; it is redirected. It may fund infrastructure, public services, debt reduction, transfers, or other forms of spending that circulate back into the economy. Whether that produces better or worse outcomes than leaving more money with top earners depends on how effectively both private and public actors use those resources. The real issue is not simply whether the rich pay more or less, but how money moves, how behavior changes, and what those changes mean for the broader economy.

The physical origin of SOT lies in the conversion of charge currents into spin accumulations or spin currents through spin-orbit coupling in materials with strong relativistic effects. When these spin currents interact with an adjacent ferromagnetic layer, they exert torques on the local magnetization, enabling deterministic switching, domain wall motion, and magnetization dynamics without the need for external magnetic fields in many cases. This capability has made SOT a central topic in both fundamental condensed matter physics and applied materials research.

Recent progress in material engineering, interface design, and device optimization has significantly enhanced the efficiency of SOT generation and control. Heavy metals, topological materials, transition metal dichalcogenides, and oxide interfaces have all been explored as effective platforms for strong spin-orbit interactions. At the same time, understanding the roles of symmetry, orbital effects, and interfacial phenomena has become essential for improving device performance and uncovering new torque mechanisms.

With continuing advances in theory, characterization techniques, and nanoscale fabrication, SOT is expected to play a key role in the development of energy-efficient and multifunctional spintronic technologies. "Estimating scores for a board of chess can be extremely difficult. Counting the pieces is a good start, but there might be situations where a player is behind on pieces but still has an advantage. 
Position is also a factor, some pieces are a lot more useful when placed in some way. To account for this the computer probably has, for each type of piece, a grid which give it a different score depending on where it is.
That's the simple part: to truly estimate how good is a board, you have to take into account what your opponent will do the following turn, and what you will do after that, etc... 
The "perfect" algorithm would simulate all possible outcome from the current board and then give it a score depending on the number of winning outcomes. This is extremely computationally expensive however, as the number of possibility grows exponentially as the simulation goes on. 
Most engines will limit themselves to simulate a few turns (like 5-6) and give estimations based on that (they look at all the possible 5-turns outcomes, rate them using a simple heuristic (like the number of pieces weighted by their position), and return the average score or something similar). 
[Edit] An other approach is to use the [monte-carlo method](_URL_0_): the computer starts with the current board and play random moves until the game is over. Then it does it again a few thousand (or million) times and use the ratio of game won/lost to estimate the state of the board. 
This works very well as a quick heuristic and is usually used in conjunction with other approach to give them a better view into the long game. (Typically the engine may simulate the next 5 turns properly and then switch to monte-carlo to go to the end of the game)"
